label: What struck the blow that shattered Straker's head?
quote: His head had been shattered by a savage blow from some heavy weapon

possibilities.quote: was just such a weapon as might, by repeated blows, have inflicted the terrible injuries

reasoning.text: The horse was in the hollow at the time, and it left alone. If someone was cutting at its leg there, as the knife and the lamed sheep suggest, a kick from a shod hoof could shatter a skull as surely as a club.

note: The means of the death has no question. The police case rests on the stick, and the entity heavy_weapon is left open at ¶35.

label: How many assailants did Straker have in the hollow?
quote: one at least of his assailants must bear his mark upon him

possibilities.quote: one at least of his assailants

reasoning.text: One blow and one cut need only one attacker, and only one man has been arrested. The plural may be the reporters' word.
If the cut and the blood are Straker's own, nothing shows that he ever got at anyone. 'Assailants' may be a word for a blow nobody saw struck.

note: Whether there was a fight at all is a thing that may not have happened. The account states it as clear at ¶35, and the reading doubts the plural at t41.2.

label: Where was the opium put into Hunter's supper?

possibilities.quote: while standing at the window, drugged his curried mutton

possibilities.value: on the path, while the maid carried it

reasoning.text: The dish was out of doors with the maid for the walk to the stables, and she met the stranger on the way.

possibilities.value: at the trainer's house, after Hunter's portion was set apart

reasoning.text: The people at the house ate the same dish unharmed, so the opium went only into the portion kept for Hunter, which may have been dosed before it left the house.

possibilities.value: in the stable, by Hunter himself

reasoning.text: Only his own supper held opium, and it was in his hands once it was handed in.

note: The place of the drugging decides whether the stranger could have done it. t37.4 lists these places, while q.who_drugged asks who and q.opium_how opens only at ¶218.

label: If the horse went in at the Mapleton gates, how did the police search miss it?
quote: It ended at the paving of asphalt which led up to the gates of the Mapleton stables.

possibilities.value: it stood among the other horses, altered so as not to be known

reasoning.text: Searchers look for the horse as described. One that no longer looked like the most remarkable horse in England could stand in a yard full of horses.

possibilities.value: it was shut away somewhere on the place that the searchers did not look

reasoning.text: Gregory says only that the stables were examined. A large establishment may have a corner that a visiting inspector would not see.

possibilities.value: it was moved off the place while the search was made

reasoning.text: The Mapleton people could have taken the horse away for the time of the police visit and brought it back afterwards.

note: The tracks at ¶124 contradict the negative search of ¶66, and Watson presses this at ¶147. How the hiding worked is a means the case turns on (t124.2).

label: Why were Straker and the horse in that hollow?
quote: at the bottom of the fatal hollow

possibilities.value: the trainer met or overtook the man leading the horse there
possibilities.quote: he was leading the horse away over the moor, when he was either met or overtaken by the trainer

possibilities.value: it lay on the way to the gypsies' camp
possibilities.quote: might he not have been leading the horse to them when he was overtaken

possibilities.value: it was chosen as a place where a light would not be seen

reasoning.text: A half-burned match lies in the mud, and Straker carried matches and a candle. A bowl in the moor hides a small light from the stables and the house.

note: The choice of place is a separate point from why the horse left the stall (q.why_led_out). The match at ¶102 turns on it.

label: What did Straker stand to gain by taking out his own horse?
quote: And yet I was at a loss to know why.

possibilities.value: money from bets laid against his own horse
possibilities.quote: laying against their own horses, through agents

possibilities.value: a payment from someone who wanted the favourite stopped

reasoning.text: Others had the strongest interest in keeping the favourite from the race, and a trainer could be paid to see to it without betting himself.

possibilities.value: the means to pay for the costly clothes on the bill in his pocket

reasoning.text: The bill for a twenty-two guinea costume was in his pocket, his wife never had such a dress, and such sums are far beyond a trainer's comfortable living.

note: The story itself asks for the motive at ¶220 and promises it at ¶225. No question here has the trainer's gain as its end: q.straker_bets asks only whether he bet.
From ¶35 to ¶40 the cravat in the dead hand points at the stranger, who has not yet been identified as Simpson.

reasoning.text: The man who came asking about the horses that evening and leaned through the stable window is the first to think of when the stall is found empty.

note: At ¶33 the reader has the stranger but no link to Simpson.

value: someone with a duplicate or stolen key

reasoning.text: The door was locked and was found open with no sign of force told. Anyone who had got hold of a key could have opened it.

note: Option in t33.2. The named key-holders do not cover it, and Simpson is only offered at ¶46.

reasoning.text: A fine blade with its cork taken off, in the hollow where the horse stood: if it was meant for the horse, the blood may be the horse's.

note: A careful reader following t82.3 would consider this, and neither possibility here covers it.
